title: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
summary: Measure a retrieval system: build a test set, compute precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG, handle judgment holes, test significance on real SciFact runs, and run online interleaving.
outcomes: Explain how a pooled test collection is built and why unjudged documents bias scores
Build a small test set: sample queries, write a graded guideline, pool every system, and check judge and LLM agreement
Compute precision, recall, P@k, R@k and F1, and use recall@k to evaluate a first stage
Compute average precision, MAP and MRR by hand and with ir_measures, and choose between them for a task
Compute DCG and nDCG with graded labels and explain why the ideal ranking comes from the qrels
Compare two systems with paired t, randomization and bootstrap tests, and report Judged@10, condensed scores and bpref
Explain why raw clicks and A/B metrics mislead and run team-draft interleaving with a sign test

lessons.title: Why you need a test collection before you can say better

blocks.md: You built a retrieval system on top of an inverted index with TF-IDF scoring. Now you change something: a new tokenizer, a different weighting, a **reranker** (a second, slower model that reorders the top results of the first ranking), or a **dense retriever** (a neural network that turns queries and documents into vectors and ranks documents by how close their vectors are). You try five queries, three look better, two look worse. Is the change an improvement? Eyeballing a handful of queries cannot answer that, because results vary enormously from query to query and you remember the striking cases.

Search evaluation turns *is it better?* into a repeatable measurement. The standard recipe, called the **Cranfield paradigm** after the aerodynamics test collection built in the UK from the late 1950s, needs a **test collection** of three things:

1. A **document collection**.
2. A set of **information needs** (TREC, the Text REtrieval Conference, calls them *topics*), each expressible as a query.
3. **Relevance judgments** (*qrels*, short for query relevance judgments): for each query and document pair, a human label, usually relevant or nonrelevant.

Relevance is judged against the **information need**, not the query words. A document that contains every query term can still be nonrelevant, and a document with none of them can be relevant. That is exactly why judgments must come from people and not from term matching.

Cranfield had 1398 abstracts (1,400 entries in the commonly distributed file, the count *Inverted indexes and TF-IDF* uses) and 225 queries, so every pair could be judged by hand. Modern collections have millions of documents, so judging every pair is impossible. TREC (run by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST, since 1992) uses **pooling**: take the top-ranked documents from many different participating systems, merge them into a pool, and have assessors judge only the pool. Everything outside the pool is unjudged.

blocks.title: How a pooled test collection is built and used

nodes.label:
Pool: union of
each run's top docs

scenes.caption: Start with topics: written statements of an information need. Each one is turned into a query and sent to every participating system.
Each system returns a ranked list (a run). Only the top of each run goes into the pool, so the pool is far smaller than the collection.
Assessors judge only pooled documents against the full topic statement. Their labels become the qrels file.
Any run can now be scored automatically against the qrels, repeatably and cheaply. This reuse is the whole point of a test collection.
The catch: a new system D may retrieve documents no pooled system found. They are unjudged, and standard tools count them as nonrelevant, so D can be under-scored.

blocks.md: Human judges also disagree. Agreement is measured with **Cohen's kappa**, which corrects raw agreement for the agreement two judges would reach by pure chance. Let $p_o$ be the fraction of documents on which the two judges agree, and $p_e$ the agreement expected if each judge labeled at random at the rates they actually used. Kappa is $p_o$ minus $p_e$, divided by 1 minus $p_e$: the share of the possible above-chance agreement that the judges achieved, so 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is chance level. For example, two judges who agree on 90% of documents and each call 20% relevant would agree by chance on 0.2 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times 0.8, or 0.68, of documents (both say relevant, or both say nonrelevant), so kappa is 0.9 minus 0.68, which is 0.22, divided by 1 minus 0.68, which is 0.32: about 0.69.

A common rule of thumb, used by Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, calls kappa above 0.8 good, 0.67 to 0.8 fair, and anything lower a dubious basis for evaluation. TREC assessors typically land in the 0.67 to 0.8 range, only *fair* agreement. Experiments that swap one judge's labels for another's change absolute scores a lot but rarely change which system ranks above which. So test collections are trustworthy for **comparing systems**, much less for absolute numbers.

blocks.caption: The two plain-text files read by trec_eval, the standard scoring program NIST distributes for TREC: the qrels and a run. Relevance 0 means judged nonrelevant; higher numbers are graded relevance.

blocks.md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

One more rule from the start: if your system has knobs (like the weights or parameters of a ranking formula), tune them on a separate **development** set of queries and report results on the **test** set. Tuning on the test queries overstates performance, because the knobs fit those particular queries rather than queries in general.

blocks.question: System D is a new dense retriever evaluated on an old pooled collection. 30% of its top-10 documents were never judged. With default trec_eval settings, what happens to those documents?
options: They are skipped, and precision is computed only over judged documents
They are counted as nonrelevant, which can make D look worse than it is
They are counted as relevant, since the system found them
trec_eval refuses to score the run until they are judged
blocks.explain: trec_eval treats documents missing from the qrels like judged-nonrelevant ones. Skipping them is only done with the -J flag, which its own help text warns against using casually. If D finds relevant documents the pool missed, it gets no credit, so its score is biased downward.

blocks.question: Two assessors judge the same pool and agree only moderately (kappa about 0.7). What does the IR literature report happens when you swap whose judgments you use?
options: Both absolute scores and the ranking of systems change drastically
Nothing changes, because kappa above 0.67 guarantees identical scores
Absolute scores can shift considerably, but the relative order of systems mostly stays the same
Only precision changes; recall is unaffected
blocks.explain: Manning, Raghavan and Schutze summarize these experiments: the choice of judge makes a considerable absolute difference but has little impact on the relative ranking of systems. That is why test collections are used to compare systems rather than to quote absolute quality.

lessons.title: Building your own test set: queries, guidelines, pools and LLM judges

blocks.md: TREC collections exist for news, the web and science, but not for your company's help center. Suppose it has 5,000 articles and a search box. To measure it the Cranfield way you must build the three parts yourself: queries, documents (you already have them) and judgments. This lesson is the recipe, in four steps, plus a fifth that is now common: letting a large language model (LLM) do some of the judging.

**Step 1: pick queries.** Take them from your search logs, because invented queries miss how people really ask. Log traffic is skewed: a few frequent queries (the *head*) account for much of it, and a long *tail* of queries is seen once. A uniform sample of query events is mostly head, so sample separately from frequency bands (head, middle, tail) and from the intents you care about, and say which bands each score covers.

How many? Lesson 6 shows why a mean over a handful of queries is noise; about 50 is the usual minimum, and more if the changes you test are small. Queries every system answers perfectly, or none answers at all, cost judging time but cannot separate systems. TREC's 2019 Deep Learning track, for example, chose which of its 200 test queries to judge by keeping candidates whose median run, scored with MS MARCO's existing sparse labels, had a reciprocal rank (1 over the rank of the first relevant result, lesson 4) above 0 and at most 0.5. NIST judged 52 of them and kept 43 for evaluation.

**Step 2: write a topic and a guideline.** For each query, write down the information need in a sentence or two (lesson 1: judges judge the need, not the words). Then fix a graded scale and define each grade with an example. TREC Deep Learning's passage scale is a good template:

- **3 Perfectly relevant**: dedicated to the query and contains the exact answer.
- **2 Highly relevant**: has some answer, but it may be unclear or hidden among extraneous information.
- **1 Related**: seems related to the query but does not answer it.
- **0 Irrelevant**: has nothing to do with the query.

blocks.title: Building a test collection for your own search system

nodes.label:
Two humans
on an overlap set

scenes.caption: Sample queries from the logs by frequency band and intent, so the tail is not drowned out by the few most frequent queries.
Write a topic (the need) and a graded guideline. Judges label against these, not against the query words.
Pool the top k of every kind of system you will compare. A pool from BM25 alone would leave a dense retriever's finds unjudged.
Humans judge the pool, with an overlap set judged twice so you can compute kappa and fix the guideline where judges disagree.
An LLM can label the rest, but only after its labels are checked against the human ones on the same pairs.

blocks.md: **Step 3: pool.** Run every system you plan to compare (say BM25, a dense retriever and a hybrid that fuses their scores), take each one's top $k$ per query, and judge the union. TREC Deep Learning 2019 pooled the top 10 of all submitted runs, then judged more documents chosen by an active-learning tool (HiCAL, which repeatedly picks the unjudged document its model thinks most likely relevant) until relevant documents were less than half of those judged. The point of going deeper is reuse: a system built next year should find few unjudged documents. Lesson 7 measures what goes wrong on SciFact when only BM25 is pooled.

**Step 4: measure agreement.** Have two people judge the same overlap set, say 10 percent of the pairs, and compute Cohen's kappa as in lesson 1. Low kappa usually means the guideline is ambiguous, so fix the wording and re-judge before labeling everything. For calibration, Thomas, Spielman, Craswell and Mitra (SIGIR 2024) computed kappa 0.52 between two groups of trained TREC assessors from Cormack et al.'s re-judging data, below the 0.67 to 0.8 quoted in lesson 1 (agreement varies with the collection and the judges), and cite crowd workers at 0.24 to 0.52 on re-judged TREC Robust documents.

**Step 5, optional: an LLM judge.** Thomas et al. describe Bing's approach: collect careful *gold* labels from real searchers, then choose the LLM and prompt whose labels agree best with them, and let that model label at scale. On 3,000 TREC Robust pairs, their 32 prompt variants reached kappa 0.20 to 0.64 against the TREC assessors, and mere paraphrases of one prompt moved kappa across a 95 percent interval of 0.50 to 0.71. UMBRELA, an open reproduction from the University of Waterloo with GPT-4o on TREC Deep Learning 2019 to 2023, got kappa 0.31 to 0.37 on the 4-grade labels, yet system rankings computed from its labels matched the human ones closely: Kendall's tau, a rank correlation where 1 means the same order of systems and 0 means unrelated orders, was 0.87 to 0.94 on nDCG@10 (a graded ranking score taught in lesson 5).

blocks.prompt: We asked a small open model, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, run locally on CPU, to judge 180 SciFact pairs: for 60 claims, one abstract the qrels mark relevant, one abstract from BM25's top 10 that the qrels do not list, and one random abstract. Will it separate the three kinds?
blocks.reveal: **Only the random ones.** It said yes to 32 of 60 qrels-relevant abstracts, 29 of 60 BM25 near misses, and 16 of 60 random abstracts. Agreement with the qrels was 59.4 percent against 52.4 percent expected by chance: kappa 0.15. Two cautions cut both ways: a near miss the qrels do not list may truly be relevant (SciFact's qrels are not exhaustive), and a model this small is far weaker than the GPT-4-class judges in the studies above. Either way, you only know because you measured.

blocks.title: How often a 0.5B local LLM said yes, by pair type (60 each)

scenes.caption: Yes when the model's score (logit) for the next word Yes beats its score for No. The judge rejects random abstracts more often but cannot tell judged-relevant abstracts from BM25's near misses: kappa 0.15 against the qrels.

blocks.code:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(2)

name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name).eval()
YES, NO = tok.encode("Yes")[0], tok.encode("No")[0]

def judge(claim, abstract):
    msg = [{"role": "system",
            "content": "You judge relevance for a scientific search engine."},
           {"role": "user", "content": f"Claim: {claim}\n\nAbstract: {abstract}"
            "\n\nDoes this abstract contain evidence that supports or "
            "refutes the claim? Answer Yes or No."}]
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msg, add_generation_prompt=True,
                                  return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(**ids).logits[0, -1]
    return float(logits[YES] - logits[NO])     # > 0 means Yes

with open("qrels.llm.txt", "w") as f:          # qrels: query 0 doc grade
    for q, d in pairs:
        f.write(f"{q} 0 {d} {int(judge(claims[q], abstracts[d]) > 0)}\n")
blocks.caption: Abridged from the script we ran (transformers on CPU, 2 threads, about 2 minutes for 180 pairs). The margin between the Yes and No logits is the judge's score; the last lines write a TREC qrels file from labels.

blocks.md: Never compare an LLM-based system against others using labels from the same or a similar LLM without a human check. Thomas et al. warn that LLM labels may favor rankers that themselves use LLMs. Before trusting LLM labels, have humans judge a sample that includes that system's results, and report the kappa. Judge biases, circularity and safe deployment are covered in *LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling*.

A home-made test collection is a sample of queries, a guideline, a pool from every system you compare, and judgments whose agreement you have measured. Each step that is skipped shows up later as noise or bias in the scores.

blocks.question: You will compare a BM25 baseline with a new reranker that uses the same LLM you plan to use as a judge. What must you do before trusting LLM labels for this comparison?
options: Nothing; LLM labels agree with humans as well as humans agree with each other
Use a larger LLM as the judge, which removes any bias
Judge only the reranker's results with the LLM and BM25's with humans
Have humans judge a sample that includes both systems' top results, and check LLM-human agreement on it
blocks.explain: The risk is that the judge rewards a system for agreeing with itself, which overall agreement numbers would not reveal. A human-judged sample covering both systems shows whether the LLM's preferences hold. A bigger model can share the same bias, and judging the systems with different labelers makes the comparison meaningless.

blocks.question: Your pool for a new collection comes only from BM25's top 20. Next quarter you test a dense retriever. What is the most likely problem?
options: Many of its top results are unjudged and count as nonrelevant, so it is under-scored
BM25's scores become inflated because its pool is too deep
Kappa between judges will drop
nDCG@10 cannot be computed for systems that were not pooled
blocks.explain: Documents a dense retriever finds that BM25 did not rank highly were never judged, and the default is to count them as nonrelevant. That is the TREC-COVID effect from lesson 6, which lesson 7 reproduces on SciFact.

lessons.title: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search

blocks.md: Take one query from the collection, q1. The qrels say **5 documents are relevant** to it. Our system returns this ranked top 10: d14, d3, d27, d8, d41, d19, d5, d33, d12, d50. Of these, d14, d27, d19 and d50 are relevant. The fifth relevant document, d9, is not in the top 10 at all. This one ranking is the running example for the whole course.
Treat the first $k$ results as a set of **retrieved** documents. Two questions matter: of what I returned, how much is relevant? And of what is relevant, how much did I return?

blocks.caption: Precision is about the quality of what you showed; recall is about coverage of what exists. The recall denominator comes from the qrels, not from the run.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the collection has 10,000 documents. Compare two systems by **accuracy** (fraction of all 10,000 relevant or nonrelevant decisions that are correct): one returns our top 6, the other returns nothing at all. Which has higher accuracy?
blocks.reveal: **They tie at 0.9995.** Each document lands in one of four outcomes: a *true positive* is relevant and returned, a *false positive* is nonrelevant but returned, a *miss* is relevant but not returned, and a *true negative* is nonrelevant and left out. Returning the top 6 gives 3 true positives, 3 false positives, 2 misses and 9992 true negatives: 9995 correct. Returning nothing gives 9995 true negatives and 5 misses: also 9995 correct. Because almost every document is nonrelevant, accuracy is dominated by true negatives and cannot tell a useful system from an empty one. Precision and recall ignore true negatives on purpose.

blocks.md: For a ranked list, compute both at every cutoff: **P@k** (precision at k) and **R@k** (recall at k). Walk down the ranking and watch how each changes.

blocks.title: Precision and recall at each cutoff for query q1

scenes.caption: Rank 1 is relevant: P@1 = 1/1 = 1.0, and R@1 = 1/5 = 0.2 because 5 documents are relevant in total.
Rank 2 is nonrelevant: precision drops to 0.5 but recall stays at 0.2. A miss can only lower precision; recall never decreases as k grows.
Rank 3 is relevant: both go up together, P@3 = 2/3 and R@3 = 0.4. Precision zig-zags while recall climbs in steps.
At k = 6 the third relevant document arrives: P@6 = 3/6 = 0.5, R@6 = 3/5 = 0.6.
At k = 10: P@10 = 0.4 and R@10 = 0.8. Recall cannot reach 1.0 here because d9 was never retrieved.

blocks.md: The two trade off. You can always reach recall 1.0 by returning every document, at terrible precision. A web searcher wants the first page to be precise and does not care about finding every relevant page; a paralegal doing legal discovery (collecting every document relevant to a lawsuit) wants high recall and tolerates scrolling through junk. **R-precision** is precision at $k = R$, the number of relevant documents; here P@5 = 2/5 = 0.4.

To combine both into one number, use the **F measure**, a *harmonic mean* of precision and recall. A harmonic mean averages the reciprocals and then flips the result back: one over $F_1$ is the average of one over P and one over R, and solving that for $F_1$ gives 2 times P times R, divided by P plus R. A small value has a huge reciprocal, so the harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller of the two, and a system cannot score well by maxing out only one. The general $F_\beta$ weights recall $\beta$ times as much as precision; the balanced version, with $\beta = 1$, is $F_1$:

blocks.caption: F1 is 2 times P times R, over P plus R. For our top 6: 2 times 0.5 times 0.6 is 0.6, and 0.6 divided by 0.5 plus 0.6, which is 1.1, gives 0.545.

blocks.title: Why F1 uses a harmonic mean

scenes.caption: Returning our top 6: precision 0.5, recall 0.6. Arithmetic mean 0.55 and F1 0.545 are close when P and R are similar.
Returning all 10,000 documents: recall 1.0, precision 0.0005. The arithmetic mean still says 0.50; F1 says 0.001, correctly calling this useless. The harmonic mean stays near the smaller value.

blocks.md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

**Recall@k for a first stage.** Many systems retrieve in two stages: a cheap first stage (BM25 or a dense retriever) fetches the top 100 or 1,000 candidates, and a slower **reranker** reorders them. A reranker cannot show a document the first stage never fetched. So measure the first stage with recall at the depth the reranker reads, R@100 or R@1000, and the final ranking with a top-heavy score such as nDCG@10 or MRR@10 (both taught in the next two lessons). In our SciFact run (lesson 7), BM25 scores higher than a small dense model on nDCG@10, 0.677 to 0.645 (a gap lesson 7 shows is not significant), yet the dense model finds slightly more relevant abstracts by depth 1,000: R@1000 0.993 against 0.977.

blocks.question: A cross-encoder reranker (a model that reads query and document together) will read the top 100 candidates from a first-stage retriever. Which metric should you use to choose between two first-stage retrievers?
options: nDCG@10 of the first stage alone
MRR@10 of the first stage alone
Recall@100
Precision@1000
blocks.explain: The reranker decides the final order, so what the first stage must do is get relevant documents into the 100 candidates. Recall@100 measures exactly that. The first stage's own top-10 order is about to be thrown away, and precision at 1000 is dominated by the many nonrelevant candidates.

blocks.question: A legal team must find every contract mentioning a clause before a court deadline, and a junior reviewer will read whatever is returned. Which metric should you optimize first?
options: Precision at 1
Recall (at a generous cutoff)
Accuracy over the whole collection
Precision at 10
blocks.explain: Missing a relevant contract is the costly error, and the team will read through extra results, so recall matters most. P@1 and P@10 measure only the top of the list, and accuracy is dominated by the huge number of true negatives.

blocks.question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
blocks.explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

lessons.title: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking

blocks.md: P@k forces you to pick a $k$ and ignores order inside the top $k$: a list with its relevant documents at ranks 1 and 2 gets the same P@10 as one with them at ranks 9 and 10. We want one number per query that rewards putting relevant documents early **and** finding all of them.

**Average precision (AP)** does this: every time you hit a relevant document, record the precision at that rank. Then average those precisions over **all** relevant documents in the qrels. A relevant document never retrieved contributes a precision of 0.

blocks.tex: \text{AP} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{k \,:\, \text{doc}_k \text{ relevant}} P@k \qquad R = \text{number of relevant docs in the qrels}
blocks.caption: AP adds up the precision at the rank of each relevant document that was retrieved, then divides by R, the number of relevant documents in the qrels; an unretrieved one adds 0.

blocks.title: Computing AP for query q1 step by step

scenes.caption: Start with no hits. The relevant set comes from the qrels and includes d9, which the run never retrieved.
k = 1, d14 is relevant: precision here is 1/1, so total becomes 1.0.
k = 2 is nonrelevant and adds nothing. k = 3, d27 is relevant: precision is 2/3 = 0.667, total 1.667.
k = 6, d19 is relevant: precision 3/6 = 0.5, total 2.167. The two misses at ranks 4 and 5 cost this hit some credit.
k = 10, d50 is relevant: precision 4/10 = 0.4, total 2.567.
Divide by all 5 relevant documents, not the 4 that were found. The missing d9 effectively contributes 0.

blocks.md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

Plot precision against recall after every rank and you get a saw-tooth **precision-recall curve**. TREC smooths it with **interpolated precision**: at recall level $r$, take the highest precision measured at any recall of $r$ or more. The reasoning, as Manning, Raghavan and Schutze put it: almost anyone would read a few more documents if that raised the share of relevant ones in what they had read, so each recall level gets the best precision still reachable, and the curve becomes a staircase that never rises to the right. The classic summary averages interpolated precision at 11 recall levels 0.0, 0.1, ..., 1.0.

scenes.caption: Actual (recall, precision) points at each hit: (0.2, 1.0), (0.4, 0.667), (0.6, 0.5), (0.8, 0.4). Recall levels in between have no measured precision yet.
Interpolate: each level takes the best precision at that recall or higher. Levels 0.0 to 0.2 get 1.0, 0.3 and 0.4 get 0.667, and so on.
Recall never reaches 0.9 because d9 was not retrieved, so levels 0.9 and 1.0 get 0. The 11-point average is 6.133 / 11 = 0.558.

blocks.md: **MAP** (mean average precision) is the arithmetic mean of AP over all queries, so every query counts equally no matter how many relevant documents it has. MAP became the main single number at TREC; trec_eval's documentation credits Chris Buckley with developing it after TREC 1 (the first TREC, held in 1992), and notes that the name is a bit redundant since AP is already per topic.

Sometimes the user needs only **one** good answer: a question-answering box, a navigational query (looking for one specific site), a known item. Then use the **reciprocal rank** (RR): $1/\text{rank}$ of the first relevant result, and 0 if none appears. Averaged over queries it is **MRR**. For four queries whose first relevant results sit at ranks 1, 3, 2 and nowhere, MRR = (1 + 0.333 + 0.5 + 0) / 4 = 0.458. **MS MARCO** (Microsoft MAchine Reading COmprehension) is a large dataset of real Bing search queries paired with passages from web pages. Its passage ranking task reports MRR@10: anything below rank 10 scores 0.

blocks.question: In q1, the relevant document d50 moves from rank 10 up to rank 7, and nothing else changes. Which metrics change?
options: P@10 and AP both increase
Only RR changes
AP increases (0.513 to 0.548); P@10 and RR stay the same
Nothing changes, because the same documents are in the top 10
blocks.explain: P@10 still counts 4 relevant in 10 slots, and RR depends only on the first relevant document, which is still d14 at rank 1. AP rewards the earlier hit: precision at that hit goes from 4/10 to 4/7, so AP becomes (1 + 0.667 + 0.5 + 0.571) / 5 = 0.548.

blocks.question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
blocks.explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

lessons.title: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first

blocks.md: Binary labels throw information away. In q1, d27 is the perfect answer, d19 and d9 are good, and d14 and d50 are only marginally useful. Give them **graded** labels: 3 (highly relevant), 2, 1, and 0 (nonrelevant). AP cannot see these grades: it would score our ranking 0.513 whether the perfect answer sits at rank 1 or at rank 3.

**Discounted cumulative gain** (DCG), introduced by Jarvelin and Kekalainen (at the SIGIR research conference in 2000, extended with a normalized version, **nDCG**, in the journal ACM TOIS in 2002), adds up a **gain** for each result, reduced by a **discount** that grows with rank, because users are less likely to look further down. The common form divides each gain by the log base 2 of the rank plus 1: rank 1 divides by 1, rank 3 by 2, rank 10 by about 3.46. The plus 1 keeps rank 1 from dividing by the log of 1, which is zero. The authors chose a logarithm so the discount falls smoothly but much more gently than dividing by the rank, since persistent users do read further down. Two gain conventions are in common use: trec_eval uses the grade itself, while the Manning, Raghavan and Schutze textbook writes the gain for a grade $g$ as $2^{g} - 1$. That gain grows exponentially with the grade (0, 1, 3 and 7 for grades 0 to 3), so a highly relevant document counts far more, and the minus 1 keeps a grade-0 document at zero gain. The formula below uses the grade itself:

blocks.caption: g_i is the grade of the document at rank i. IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ranking: all judged documents sorted by grade, best first. Dividing by it puts every query on a 0 to 1 scale.

blocks.title: DCG@10 for q1, then the ideal ranking

scenes.caption: Our ranking's grades at ranks 1 to 10, with the discount for each rank. Rank 1 is undiscounted; rank 10 keeps only 0.289 of its gain.
Multiply grade by discount. The grade-3 document at rank 3 is worth 3 x 0.5 = 1.5; at rank 1 it would have been worth 3.0.
Running sum: DCG@5 = 2.500 and DCG@10 = 3.501. On its own this number has no fixed scale, so it cannot be compared across queries.
The ideal ranking sorts every judged document by grade, including d9 (grade 2) that our run missed: 3, 2, 2, 1, 1. Its DCG@10 is 6.079.
Normalize: nDCG@10 = 3.501 / 6.079 = 0.576, and nDCG@5 = 2.500 / 6.079 = 0.411. A perfect ranking always scores 1.

blocks.title: How much one result is worth at each rank

scenes.caption: Grade 1: both gain forms coincide, since 2^1 - 1 = 1. The log discount falls much more gently than reciprocal rank, so rank 10 still counts for 0.29.
Grade 3: the exponential form gives 7 instead of 3, so one highly relevant document outweighs several marginal ones. Which form you use changes the score.

blocks.prompt: Swap d14 (grade 1) and d27 (grade 3), so the perfect answer is at rank 1. What happens to AP and to nDCG@10?
blocks.reveal: **AP is unchanged at 0.513**: both documents count as relevant, and relevant documents still sit at ranks 1, 3, 6 and 10. **nDCG@10 rises from 0.576 to 0.740** (linear gain), or from 0.523 to 0.790 with exponential gain. Only a graded metric can tell that the best answer moved to the top.

blocks.md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

In practice you compute metrics with a library rather than by hand. **ir_measures** (from the Terrier team at the University of Glasgow) gives one interface over trec_eval (through pytrec_eval) and other back ends. Feeding it q1's qrels and ranking reproduces every hand-computed value in this course, and a twenty-line nDCG shows the one rule that matters: the ideal comes from the qrels.

blocks.code:
import math, ir_measures
from ir_measures import P, AP, RR, nDCG

qrels = {"q1": {"d14": 1, "d27": 3, "d19": 2, "d50": 1, "d9": 2,
                "d3": 0, "d8": 0, "d41": 0, "d5": 0, "d33": 0, "d12": 0}}
ranking = ["d14", "d3", "d27", "d8", "d41", "d19", "d5", "d33", "d12", "d50"]
run = {"q1": {d: 10.0 - i for i, d in enumerate(ranking)}}  # higher = better

print(ir_measures.calc_aggregate([P@10, AP, RR, nDCG@10], qrels, run))

def ndcg_at_k(ranking, grades, k=10):
    dcg = sum(grades.get(d, 0) / math.log2(i + 2)       # rank i+1
              for i, d in enumerate(ranking[:k]))
    ideal = sorted(grades.values(), reverse=True)[:k]   # from the qrels
    idcg = sum(g / math.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0

print(round(ndcg_at_k(ranking, qrels["q1"]), 3))
blocks.caption: Run as shown (ir_measures 0.4.3). Output: P@10 0.4, AP 0.5133, RR 1.0, nDCG@10 0.5760, then 0.576 from the plain-Python version. Scores are written so that higher means better, since trec_eval ignores ranks.

blocks.md: For q1 the two gains, the grade $g_i$ and $2^{g_i} - 1$, give nDCG@10 of 0.576 and 0.523. Always state the gain and the cutoff when you report nDCG. **BEIR**, a widely used benchmark of 18 retrieval datasets that tests models *zero-shot* (on collections they were never trained on), reports nDCG@10 on every dataset because it works with both binary and graded judgments.
nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

nDCG's log discount is one model of how far users read. Other metrics model the user differently, for example ERR, which assumes a user stops once satisfied; they are compared in *Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR*.

blocks.question: Two teams score the same run on the same qrels and report nDCG@10 of 0.576 and 0.523. Neither has a bug. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One used a natural log instead of log base 2 in the discount
One used linear gain g and the other exponential gain 2^g - 1
One computed nDCG@5 by mistake
nDCG is randomized, so small differences are expected
blocks.explain: These are exactly q1's values under the two gain conventions. Changing the log base alone would not change nDCG at all, since the same constant factor appears in DCG and IDCG and cancels. nDCG@5 is 0.411 here, and nDCG is deterministic.

blocks.question: A reranker reorders a run's top 10 so the grades go from 1,0,3,0,0,2,0,0,0,1 to 3,2,1,1,0,0,0,0,0,0. What nDCG@10 does it reach, and why not 1.0?
options: 1.0, because the top 10 is now in perfect order
Below 1.0, because d9 (grade 2) is still missing and IDCG includes it
Below 1.0, because nDCG penalizes reordering
Exactly 0.576, because the same documents are retrieved
blocks.explain: Reordering cannot add documents. The ideal ranking from the qrels is 3,2,2,1,1, so this list (3,2,1,1) still loses gain for the missing grade-2 document. Only a better first-stage retriever that finds d9 could reach 1.0.

lessons.title: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, significance

blocks.md: You now have metrics. The hard part is using them to decide whether system B really beats system A. Three things routinely mislead people: **unjudged documents**, **per-query variance**, and **tool defaults**.

**Holes in the judgments.** Pools come from the systems that existed when the collection was built. A new kind of system can retrieve relevant documents that nobody judged, and they count as nonrelevant. The BEIR authors measured this on **TREC-COVID** (a TREC collection built in 2020 from scientific articles about COVID-19): they judged 980 extra query-document pairs that various systems put in their top 10 but annotators had never seen, then rescored everything. The systems in the figure: **BM25** (Best Matching 25), the standard *lexical* ranking function, meaning it matches query words, refining TF-IDF with capped term counts and document length normalization; **docT5query**, which uses the T5 language model to generate likely queries for each document, appends them to it and then ranks with BM25; and **ANCE** and **TAS-B**, two dense retrievers.

blocks.title: TREC-COVID nDCG@10 before and after filling judgment holes

scenes.caption: With the original judgments, the dense retriever ANCE (0.654) looks slightly worse than BM25 (0.656). Lexical systems had 6.4% and 2.8% unjudged top-10 hits; TAS-B had 31.8%.
After judging the holes, lexical systems barely move (BM25 +0.012, docT5query +0.001) but ANCE jumps +0.081 to 0.735 and beats BM25. The pool was biased toward lexical matching.

blocks.md: **Metrics for incomplete judgments.** Three tools help when judging more is not possible. First, report the share of each run's top 10 that was judged, often called **Judged@10**; a low value warns that the score is unreliable. Second, **condensed lists**: delete unjudged documents from the run and score what remains (trec_eval's -J flag, ir_measures' `judged_only`). Third, **bpref** (binary preference, Buckley and Voorhees, SIGIR 2004), which uses only judged documents: for each relevant document it counts how many judged nonrelevant documents rank above it.

blocks.caption: R is the number of relevant documents, N the number of judged nonrelevant ones, and the sum runs over retrieved relevant documents r. This is the form in trec_eval's source.

blocks.title: q1 when d41 and d33 were never judged

scenes.caption: Same q1 ranking, but d41 and d33 are missing from the qrels. Judged@10 = 8/10 = 0.8. Default scoring treats both as nonrelevant, so AP stays 0.513 and nDCG@10 0.576.
Condensed list: delete the holes. d19 moves up from rank 6 to 5 and d50 from 10 to 8, so AP rises to 0.553 and nDCG@10 to 0.590 with nothing new learned.
bpref: R = 5 relevant, N = 4 judged nonrelevant, so the divisor is 4. d14 has none above (1), d27 has one (0.75), d19 two (0.5), d50 four (0). Sum 2.25 / 5 = 0.45; with full judgments it is 0.44.

blocks.md: Each fix has a known cost. Condensed lists reward a system for retrieving unjudged documents, because deleting them moves its judged documents up, which is why trec_eval's help text says not to use -J unless you know what you are doing. bpref barely moves when judgments are removed, which is its purpose, but it ignores everything unjudged, including relevant documents the pool missed. Lesson 7 runs all three on SciFact.

**Per-query variance.** One system's AP typically ranges widely across queries (Manning et al. cite 0.1 to 0.7), and scores for one query usually agree more across systems than scores for different queries within one system. A mean over a few queries is therefore noisy; about 50 information needs is the usual rule-of-thumb minimum. Look at the per-query differences, not just the means.

blocks.title: Per-query AP for systems A and B (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Illustrative numbers. MAP for A is 0.368 and for B is 0.430, so B looks 17% better on average.
But B is worse on 6 of the 8 queries. Its whole advantage comes from q4, where A scored 0.10 and B scored 0.70.
Drop q4 and A wins, 0.406 to 0.391. A paired t-test over the 8 differences gives p = 0.44 and a sign test p = 0.29: no evidence that B is better in general.

blocks.md: Compare systems with a **paired** test over queries: each query is scored by both systems, so test the per-query differences. Each test returns a **p-value**: the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two systems were really equally good. A small p-value (conventionally below 0.05) is evidence of a real difference; p = 0.44 is not. Below are the classic three (sign, t, Wilcoxon) and the **randomization test**.

The **sign test** only counts wins: if the systems were equally good, each query would be a fair coin flip, so it asks how likely a split at least as lopsided as ours would be. B wins 2 of 8. Of the 256 equally likely win and loss patterns over 8 queries, 1 has no wins, 8 have one win and 28 have two (the ways to choose 2 queries out of 8), so the chance of 2 or fewer wins is 37 / 256 = 0.145, and doubling it to allow either system to be the lucky one gives 0.29. The **paired t-test** also uses the sizes: it asks how many standard errors the mean difference is from zero. Here the mean difference is 0.0625, the standard deviation of the 8 differences is 0.218, and the standard error is 0.218 over the square root of 8, or 0.077, so t = 0.81, a value the t distribution with 7 degrees of freedom (one fewer than the 8 differences, since their mean was estimated from them) produces often by chance (p = 0.44). The **Wilcoxon signed-rank test** sits between them: it ranks the differences by size, ignoring sign, and adds up the ranks of the wins, so one huge win counts only as the top rank.

blocks.code:
import itertools
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

d = np.array([-0.03, -0.02, 0.02, 0.60, -0.03, -0.01, -0.02, -0.01])  # B minus A
t = d.mean() / (d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d)))
print("t =", t.round(2), " p =", (2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df=7)).round(2))

hits = 0                                  # randomization test, exact
for signs in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=8):
    if abs((d * np.array(signs)).mean()) >= abs(d.mean()) - 1e-12:
        hits += 1
print(hits, "of 256 sign patterns  p =", round(hits / 256, 3))
blocks.caption: Run as shown. Output: t = 0.81, p = 0.44 (the two-sided tail of the t distribution with 7 degrees of freedom), then 250 of 256 sign patterns, p = 0.977.

blocks.md: The **randomization test** asks the null hypothesis directly: if A and B were interchangeable, each query's difference could equally well have had the opposite sign. With 8 queries there are $2^8 = 256$ sign patterns, so we can enumerate them all and count those whose mean is at least as far from zero as 0.0625. Here 250 of 256 are, p = 0.977. The outlier explains why: q4's 0.60 alone adds 0.075 to the mean, so nearly any pattern stays that far from zero. The data say one query moved a lot, not that B is better. Note that the t-test (p = 0.44) and the randomization test (p = 0.977) disagree here: with 8 queries and one outlier the t-test's normal approximation is poor. The agreement reported next was found on TREC runs with 50 topics.

Smucker, Allan and Carterette (CIKM 2007) ran five tests on every pair of runs from TRECs 3 and 5 to 8. The t-test, the randomization test and the **bootstrap** (resample queries with replacement many times and look at the spread of the mean difference) largely agreed; the sign and Wilcoxon tests disagreed with them, and the authors say those two should no longer be used to test a difference in means. Lesson 7 runs the t, randomization and bootstrap tests on real SciFact runs. Two habits matter beyond the p-value: report the mean difference with a confidence interval, so readers see how large it may be, and if you test many variants against one baseline, some will pass p < 0.05 by luck, so correct for the number of tests (Bonferroni divides 0.05 by it). Effect sizes and testing many systems at once are in *Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR*; bootstrap intervals and Bonferroni and Holm corrections in *Avoiding overfitting to a public query set*.
Then read the failing queries; a single outlier like q4 often reveals a bug or a judgment hole rather than a better model.

blocks.code:
# per-query scores (-q), and count queries with no results as 0 (-c)
trec_eval -q -c -m map -m ndcg_cut.10 -m recip_rank qrels.txt run.txt

# graded qrels: treat only grade >= 2 as relevant for binary metrics
trec_eval -l 2 -m map qrels.txt run.txt
blocks.caption: trec_eval flags from its own help text. -l sets the minimum grade counted as relevant (default 1).

blocks.md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

**Offline is not the whole story.** Judges cannot always guess real users' intents, and judging is slow and costly, so production search teams also test on live traffic. The last lesson covers online evaluation: clicks, A/B tests and interleaving.

A test collection is a measuring instrument with known biases. Report the metric, cutoff and gain you used, look at per-query results, test significance with paired tests, and be suspicious when a genuinely new kind of system loses on an old pool.

blocks.question: Your new dense retriever scores 0.05 nDCG@10 below BM25 on a collection whose pool was built mostly from lexical systems a decade ago. What should you do before concluding it is worse?
options: Nothing; nDCG@10 already accounts for unjudged documents
Switch to P@10, which is not affected by unjudged documents
Measure how many of its top-10 documents are unjudged, and judge a sample of them
Re-run with trec_eval -J and report that number as the true score
blocks.explain: Unjudged documents count as nonrelevant in nDCG and in P@10 alike. Measuring the hole rate and judging a sample, as BEIR did on TREC-COVID, tells you whether the gap is real. The -J flag drops unjudged documents, which inflates scores in a different way and is not comparable.

blocks.question: B beats A on MAP, 0.43 versus 0.37, over 8 queries. B wins on 2 queries and loses on 6. Which conclusion is justified?
options: B is better: MAP is the standard measure
Not established yet: check per-query differences with a paired test and add queries
A is better because it wins more queries
They are identical because 8 queries is too few to compute MAP
blocks.explain: A mean driven by one or two queries is fragile, and with 8 queries neither a t-test (p = 0.44) nor a sign test (p = 0.29) supports a general claim. Counting wins alone is also not a valid conclusion. Use more queries (about 50 is a common minimum) and a paired test.

blocks.question: On q1, two retrieved documents are unjudged. Scored as a condensed list, AP goes from 0.513 to 0.553. What does that increase mean?
options: Nothing about quality: deleting the unjudged documents moved later relevant documents up
The two unjudged documents were probably relevant
The run is better than the default score showed, so 0.553 is the true AP
Condensed lists fix the IDCG, so the new score is more accurate
blocks.explain: Nothing new was learned about the run. Condensing only removed two ranks, so d19 and d50 sit higher and earn more precision. That is the bias of condensed lists: retrieving many unjudged documents can raise a score. Whether those documents are relevant is unknown until someone judges them.

lessons.title: Measuring two real systems on SciFact: tests, intervals, pool bias

blocks.md: Time to use everything on real data. The collection is BEIR's **SciFact**, the one *BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting* tuned on: 5,183 scientific abstracts, and as queries 300 test claims such as "0-dimensional biomaterials lack inductive properties", with about 1.1 relevant abstracts per claim. System A is that course's BM25 setup: default parameters ($k_1 = 1.2$ sets how fast repeated terms saturate, $b = 0.75$ how strongly long documents are penalized), Porter stemming, a 33-word stop list, and title plus abstract as one field. Other BM25 setups score SciFact differently. System B is a small dense retriever, **all-MiniLM-L6-v2**, a sentence-embedding model that maps each text to 384 numbers; documents are ranked by cosine similarity to the claim. In our run, encoding the corpus took about a minute on two CPU threads.

blocks.title: SciFact test, 300 claims: BM25 vs MiniLM

scenes.caption: BM25 scores 0.677 nDCG@10, matching the BM25 course, and MiniLM 0.645. A 0.032 gap in BM25's favor, before asking whether it is real.
As a first stage the order flips in our run: MiniLM finds slightly more relevant abstracts by depth 100 and 1,000, by margins too small to call. Which system is better depends on the job (lesson 3).

blocks.md: Now look per query. Of 300 claims, 162 have identical nDCG@10 under both systems, MiniLM wins 65 and loses 73. The mean difference (MiniLM minus BM25) is -0.032, the standard deviation of the 300 differences is 0.318, and the standard error, 0.318 divided by the square root of 300, is 0.018. Most queries do not move because, with about one relevant abstract per claim, nDCG@10 changes only when that abstract crosses a rank (*BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting* found the same when tuning).

blocks.prompt: The gap is 0.032 nDCG@10 over 300 queries, with a standard error of 0.018. Does a paired test say BM25 is significantly better (p below 0.05)?
blocks.reveal: **No.** Paired t-test p = 0.081; randomization test p = 0.083; a paired bootstrap 95 percent interval for MiniLM minus BM25 is [-0.069, 0.004], which includes 0. The three agree, as Smucker et al. found on TREC runs. The sign test (65 against 73) gives p = 0.55 and the Wilcoxon test p = 0.086. The honest summary: BM25 is ahead by 0.032 on SciFact, and 300 queries cannot rule out a tie.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np, ir_measures
from ir_measures import nDCG
from scipy import stats

qrels = list(ir_measures.read_trec_qrels("qrels.test.txt"))
def per_query(path):
    run = ir_measures.read_trec_run(path)
    return {m.query_id: m.value for m in ir_measures.iter_calc([nDCG@10], qrels, run)}
a, b = per_query("bm25.run"), per_query("minilm.run")
qs = sorted({q.query_id for q in qrels})
d = np.array([b.get(q, 0) - a.get(q, 0) for q in qs])   # MiniLM minus BM25

print(len(d), d.mean().round(4), (d > 0).sum(), (d < 0).sum())
print("t-test p", stats.ttest_rel(d, np.zeros_like(d)).pvalue.round(3))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                  # randomization test
signs = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(100_000, len(d)))
null = (signs * d).mean(axis=1)
print("randomization p", (np.abs(null) >= abs(d.mean())).mean().round(3))

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                  # paired bootstrap
boot = d[rng.integers(0, len(d), size=(10_000, len(d)))].mean(axis=1)
print("95% CI", np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]).round(3))
blocks.caption: Run as shown on our run files (ir_measures, scipy). Output: 300 -0.0321 65 73; t-test p 0.081; randomization p 0.083; 95% CI [-0.069 0.004].

blocks.title: Where -0.032 falls if the systems were equal

x.label: mean nDCG@10 gap, MiniLM minus BM25

scenes.caption: With 300 queries, chance alone spreads the mean difference with a standard error of 0.018, so -0.032 is only 1.75 standard errors out: p about 0.08.
If 1,200 queries had the same per-query spread, the standard error would halve to 0.009 and the same gap would be 3.5 standard errors out. Small gaps need many queries.

blocks.md: **Pool bias, measured.** Now pretend SciFact had been built by pooling only BM25's top 10. Every pooled abstract gets its SciFact label (relevant if in the qrels, otherwise judged nonrelevant), and everything outside the pool is unjudged. The BM25 pool contains 268 of the 339 relevant pairs. Then score both systems against these pooled judgments and compare with the full qrels.

blocks.title: SciFact nDCG@10 under different judgment sets

scenes.caption: Full SciFact qrels: BM25 0.677, MiniLM 0.645, a gap of 0.032.
Pool from BM25's top 10 only: BM25 rises to 0.686, MiniLM drops to 0.616, and the gap more than doubles to 0.069. Only 34 percent of MiniLM's top 10 is judged.
Same BM25 pool, condensed lists (unjudged deleted): MiniLM 0.691 now edges past BM25 0.686 in our run. The bias flips the other way.
Pool the top 10 of both systems (16.6 abstracts per claim): BM25 0.679, MiniLM 0.648, gap 0.031, close to the full-qrels gap.

blocks.md: Two effects stack. MiniLM's finds outside BM25's top 10 are unjudged and count as misses, so its score drops. BM25's score rises because relevant abstracts outside BM25's top 10 vanish from the qrels and so from the ideal ranking, which shrinks IDCG. bpref, which ignores unjudged documents, gave 0.544 to BM25 and 0.542 to MiniLM on the BM25 pool, a near tie. Only pooling both systems recovered a gap close to the true one.

Simplified: this treats SciFact's qrels as the truth, but they are not exhaustive either, so an abstract outside them may still be relevant. The experiment shows the direction and size of pool bias for systems missing from the pool, not exact true scores.

Report a difference with its paired test or confidence interval, check Judged@10 for every system, and pool every kind of system you compare. In our SciFact simulation a BM25-only pool doubled BM25's lead, and condensed lists erased it.

blocks.question: In our run, a paired bootstrap 95 percent interval for MiniLM minus BM25 on SciFact is [-0.069, 0.004]. Which statement is justified?
options: MiniLM is significantly worse, because most of the interval is negative
The systems are equally good, because the interval contains 0
The interval is invalid because nDCG is bounded between 0 and 1
The data are consistent with anything from BM25 ahead by about 0.07 to a tiny MiniLM lead; more queries are needed to decide
blocks.explain: An interval containing 0 means the test cannot rule out no difference; it does not prove equality. Most of it being negative is suggestive, not significant. Bootstrapping a mean of bounded per-query scores is standard practice.

blocks.question: With the BM25-only pool, why did BM25's own nDCG@10 rise from 0.677 to 0.686?
options: Pooling adds new relevant documents to BM25's run
Relevant abstracts that no pooled run found dropped out of the qrels, lowering the ideal DCG
The pool assigns higher grades to BM25's documents
Unjudged documents count as relevant by default
blocks.explain: nDCG divides by the DCG of the ideal ranking built from the qrels. Relevant abstracts outside the pool are no longer known, so the ideal gets smaller and the same BM25 ranking captures a larger fraction of it. The run did not change; the yardstick shrank.

lessons.title: Online evaluation: clicks, position bias, A/B tests and interleaving

blocks.md: A team ships a new ranker to half its users. A week later the new half has a slightly lower click-through rate. Is the ranker worse? Maybe. Maybe users found the answer in the result snippet and did not need to click, or the old half happened to include more heavy users. Online evaluation measures real people's behavior on live traffic, which judges cannot simulate, but behavior is a noisy and biased signal. This lesson shows why, and the paired design, **interleaving**, that copes with it.

**Clicks are biased judgments.** Joachims, Granka, Pan, Hembrooke and Gay (SIGIR 2005) recorded where students looked and clicked while answering questions with Google. In a *swapped* condition the top two results were secretly exchanged. On results pages where relevance judges rated the second result as more relevant, users still clicked only the first result 10 times and only the second 7 times. The authors call this **trust bias**: users trust the engine's order. When the whole top 10 was reversed, the average rank of a click went from 2.66 to 4.03 and clicks per query fell from 0.80 to 0.64. Clicks depend on relevance, but also on position and on how good the rest of the page is.

Correcting clicks for position bias (click models such as the cascade model, which assumes users scan down and click the first attractive result, and inverse propensity weighting, which up-weights clicks at rarely seen ranks) is the subject of *Click models and unbiased learning to rank*. Here we only need the consequence: a raw click count is not a relevance label.

**A/B tests.** Randomly assign each user to A or B, then compare **absolute metrics** averaged per user: *abandonment rate* (share of queries with no click), *reformulation rate* (share followed by a rewritten query), *clicks per query*, *time to first click*, and *max reciprocal rank* (1 over the rank of the top-most clicked result). Radlinski, Kurup and Joachims (CIKM 2008) tested these on arXiv.org's search engine against rankers whose order of quality was known by construction: Orig, a degraded Flat, and Rand (Flat with its top 11 shuffled); and Orig against Swap2 and Swap4 (two or four top-5 results swapped with lower ones).

blocks.title: arXiv.org abandonment rate by ranker (Radlinski et al. 2008)

scenes.caption: Orig, Flat, Rand: abandonment 0.680, 0.725, 0.726 (about plus or minus 0.021 each). Worse rankers lose more queries, as expected, but Flat and Rand look identical.
Orig, Swap2, Swap4, a few weeks earlier: 0.704, 0.680, 0.698. The degraded Swap2 looks best. With these sample sizes, noise exceeds the quality gaps.

blocks.md: Across both comparisons, no absolute metric reliably reflected the known order. Apart from max reciprocal rank, not even the large differences (Orig against Rand, Orig against Swap4) were consistently significant. Orig's own abandonment rate also differed significantly between data collected over Christmas and in February, so population shifts can be as large as the quality differences being measured.

**Interleaving** turns the comparison into a paired one. Each user gets a single list that mixes A's and B's results, and their clicks reveal which system's results they preferred, on the same query, at the same moment. **Team-draft interleaving** (Radlinski et al. 2008) works like picking sides for a game. Two captains, A and B, take turns. On each round, whichever team has fewer documents picks next; when they are level, a coin decides. The picking team adds its highest-ranked document not already shown, and that document belongs to its team.

blocks.title: Team-draft interleaving of A = d1 d2 d3 d4 and B = d2 d5 d1 d6

scenes.caption: Teams are level at 0 and 0, so a coin decides: B. B drafts its top document, d2.
A has fewer, so A picks without a coin. Its top document d1 is unused, so d1 goes to team A.
Level at 1 and 1; the coin says A. A's next document d2 is already shown, so A takes d3.
B is behind, so B picks its best unused document, d5.
Level at 2 and 2; the coin says B. d1 is taken, so B adds d6. Every B document is now shown, so drafting stops and d4 is never shown.
The user clicks d5 and d3. d3 is on team A and d5 on team B: 1 click each, so this query is a tie and gives no preference.

blocks.code:
import random

def team_draft(A, B, rng):
    shown, team = [], {}
    while any(d not in team for d in A) and any(d not in team for d in B):
        na = sum(1 for t in team.values() if t == "A")
        nb = len(team) - na
        pick_a = na < nb or (na == nb and rng.random() < 0.5)   # coin on ties
        src, name = (A, "A") if pick_a else (B, "B")
        doc = next(d for d in src if d not in team)    # its best unused doc
        shown.append(doc)
        team[doc] = name
    return shown, team

def credit(team, clicked):
    a = sum(team[d] == "A" for d in clicked)
    b = sum(team[d] == "B" for d in clicked)
    return "A" if a > b else "B" if b > a else "tie"

shown, team = team_draft(["d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"], ["d2", "d5", "d1", "d6"],
                         random.Random(3))
print(shown, team)
print(credit(team, ["d5", "d3"]))

blocks.md: Per query, the system with more clicked team members wins; equal counts are a tie and are dropped. Over many queries, count wins for A and for B and apply a **binomial sign test**: under no preference each win is a fair coin. A document both systems rank highly, like d2, goes to whichever team drafted it, and the coin makes that fair on average. Radlinski et al. note that with team-draft, a user who clicks at random produces as many preferences for A as for B in expectation, which an earlier method, balanced interleaving, does not guarantee when the two rankings are nearly identical.

Did it work? On arXiv.org, for all six pairs of rankers, the winner by team-draft and by balanced interleaving matched the known order, and no test pointed the wrong way. For Orig against Rand, Orig won 55.6 percent of 1,095 team-draft queries and Rand 29.8 percent (the rest tied): about 609 wins to 326, a sign test p near $10^{-20}$. Overall 20 of the 24 interleaving tests were significant at 95 percent, the other four at 90. Chapelle, Joachims, Radlinski and Yue (ACM TOIS 2012) confirmed this on Bing and Yahoo! search: interleaving agreed with expert judgments, and on Yahoo!, for five of six pairs of rankers, it needed over an order of magnitude fewer queries than Clicks@1, the best absolute metric there.

Absolute online metrics compare different users at different times, so user variation swamps small quality differences. Interleaving shows both systems to the same user on the same query and asks which one they preferred, the online version of a paired test.

Interleaving says which system users prefer on a result page, and it needs clicks to work. It cannot measure effects beyond one page, such as revenue or whether users come back next week; those still need an A/B test.

blocks.question: Why does interleaving usually detect a quality difference with far fewer queries than an A/B test on click-through rate?
options: Interleaving shows users twice as many results
Interleaving uses expert judgments in addition to clicks
Each interleaved query compares both systems for the same user and query, so differences between users and queries cancel out
A/B tests discard queries without clicks
blocks.explain: An A/B test compares averages over different people, so variation between users and between queries adds noise to the difference. Interleaving pairs the comparison on query and user, the same reason a paired t-test beats an unpaired one. Chapelle et al. conjecture exactly this, plus the more direct preference signal.

blocks.question: In team-draft interleaving, both A and B rank d2 first. The coin gives d2 to team B, and the user clicks only d2. What is recorded for this query?
options: A tie, because both systems ranked d2 first
A win for B; over many queries the coin gives such shared documents to A and B equally often
A win for A, because A's ranking was used to build the list
Nothing, because shared documents are excluded from interleaving
blocks.explain: Credit follows the team that drafted the document. A single impression is unfair to A, but the coin makes A draft shared documents half the time, so the bias cancels over many queries.
